subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE
speechtext: I desire to direct to the Minister of National Defence a question of which I have given him verbal notice. What are the reasons of security which prevent the Canadian people from knowing the extent of the casualties in France, having regard to the fact that Lieutenant-General Bradley, at a press conference on the beachhead on June 17, disclosed to the war correspondents present that American casualties for the first eleven days of the invasion totalled 16,883, including 3,283 known dead, and 12,600 wounded? If there is to be one rule for the people of the United States and another for the Canadian people, I think the position should be clarified, and we should be given convincing reasons why they disclosed the casualty figures and the Canadian government refuses to do likewise.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE
speechtext:
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I wish my hon. friend and the house to note that it was not the United States government that made the statement which was given; it. was the field commander. As a result of arrangements which were made prior to operations in the Mediterranean in July last year, it was agreed that the actual number of casualties would be released only if and when the commander in the field who is responsible for the conduct of the operations feels that such release will not prejudice the progress of the operation. I have always considered this arrangement binding, and I have never per-

Dominion Coal Company
mitted a release of casualty figures which might be regarded as in any way endangering the security of our forces. Any releases authorized by me have been the subject of prior consultation with our allies.	_
When the hon. member asked the question on Friday I told the house that nothing but security reasons prevented these figures from being announced, but that I would have to consult our allies before an announcement could be made. I must say I was very much surprised to learn on Saturday morning that an announcement had been made from the field respecting United States casualties. The house will recognize, I am sure, that I would want to take instant action in respect of it. I cabled Canadian military headquarters, as I indicated on Friday that I would do. I stated that since the totals had been announced for the United States I did not see why we could not announce the Canadian casualties as well, and I asked that communication be made with the appropriate officers so as to ensure concurrent statements on matters of this kind in the future. The reply I received this morning gave the circumstances under which the announcement was made by the field commander, which I will not disclose. The reply does, however, state that there is an agreement that no additional statement will be made public at present and that we shall be advised regarding any further announcement so that a simultaneous release can be made in Canada.
When I received this reply this morning. I telephoned to Canadian military headquarters and pointed out to them the incongruity of one country issuing a statement and others not doing so. And questioning whether an agreement should be made under these circumstances, they advised that the request had come from responsible officers connected with the combined operations, and very strongly advised that it would be definitely regarded by those who are in charge as a breach of security if figures were released by Canada at this time. I may say that figures have not been given by any of the other principal allies, that I have heard of. -I have given full consideration to the matter and under the circumstances I am not prepared to overrule the judgment of those who are on the spot, who are closer to the position than we here can possibly be. They know the detriment which might be caused to the troops -and that includes Canadian troops-and to the success of the operation itself by the giving of this information. I can only ask the house and the public to accept their judgment, as I do, and to await the announcement of the number of casualties whenever it is considered, by those in charge, that they may be safely released.
May I say further that casualties, no matter how limited they may be, are always too many. However, there are two statements I can make which I think should afford considerable relief. In the first place, in these almost two weeks of fighting in France, the Canadian casualties are moderate and below the total number estimated for the initial phase of the operation. That is gratifying and must be given at this time without amplification. The numbers will gradually disclose themselves by the publishing of lists as time goes by; but, as they explained to me, what they want to avoid is the giving out of the number of casualties for any particular phase of the operation.
The second point is that in this operation the system of reporting individual casualties is functioning, I think, with maximum efficiency. I can assure the house that almost every casualty sustained up to Friday last has been reported directly to the next of kin, and they are being kept informed of the progress of those who are wounded. It is proposed that this service shall continue to be given to the next of kin without interruption. I think we can be sure that they as well as the public are conscious of the security restrictions and would not insist that casualty figures should be given out if responsible authorities on the ground consider it inadvisable.

subtopic: DOMINION COAL COMPANY-NON-OPERATION OF MINES ON SATURDAY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DOMINION COAL COMPANY-NON-OPERATION OF MINES ON SATURDAY
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the
Dominion Coal Company

Minister of Munitions and Supply arising out out of a telegram received from Local' 4530, United Mineworkers of Nova Scotia, protesting against the action of the Dominion Coal company in leaving their mines idle on Saturdays. In view of the anticipated fuel emergency in the coming winter, as exemplified by the minister's warnings to the public to get their fuel stocks early, will the minister check with the Dominion Coal company as to the possibility of continuous employment in the mines, including Saturdays? Secondly, is he in a position to take any action with respect to the second part of the telegram, namely, the miners demand for remuneration for the time lost through the company's action in keeping the mines idle?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: DOMINION COAL COMPANY-NON-OPERATION OF MINES ON SATURDAY
speechtext:
The hon. member was good
enough to give me notice of the question, and I have obtained the pertinent facts, which I think should be placed before the house. I must give them at some length.
I must say at once that every ton of coal that can be mined in Nova Scotia is required to meet the present coal shortage. The record of coal production in Nova Scotia during past months has been anything but satisfactory. The Department of Munitions and Supply and the Dominion Coal company as a whole are making desperate efforts to improve the situation. The salient points remain and can be noted as follows:
1.	Daily production is declining from a normal 18,000 tons per day; the average at the present time is nearer 12,000 tons per day.
2.	The output per man per day has decreased from 2-67 tons in 1939 to 1-73 tons per man per day for April of this year.
3.	Absenteeism has increased from 14-9 per
cent in January of this year to 29-7 per cent for the month of May.	,
As a further example of the difficulties encountered, when retroactive wages were paid out on May 15, 1944, covering the order of the national war labour board, absenteeism reached a high of 41-4 per cent. This figure has mot been included in the above averages.
Another case is at No. 24 colliery (Caledonia) ; the mine was idle for four days, the reason given that the miners were looking for a woman who had wandered away from home. It was found that the number of men looking for this person, out of a total labour force at this mine of 468, did not amount to more then twenty on May 11 and about eight on May 12. There is no record of any men seeking the lost person on May 13 and 15,

and the mine was idle for the four days and not one man asked permission to absent himself from work.
A recent survey of mining labour in the Cape Breton area indicates that there are over 600 men who are either qualified to obtain second class certificates as miners or who already have certificates but will not transfer from datal work to contract work at the coal face. The management have not to date induced these men to take over the actual productive labour in the mines, yet a substantial number of alternate workers could be found to take the place of these qualified miners now on non-productive mining work.
In an endeavour to remedy the situation the management sought permission to establish a five day week at certain of the collieries to see whether or not it would improve matters. This resulted in a telegram sent me by the Caledonia local asking that the government pay them for the shifts lost on Saturday, June 3, and Saturday, June 10.
The facts of the matter are: the company have attempted to work Caledonia mine on Friday afternoon and Saturday morning shifts against increasing absenteeism indicative of the reluctance of the producers to work on these two shifts.	The average week-end
absenteeism producers during May at the Caledonia collieries on Friday afternoon amounted to 64-5 per cent and on Saturday morning shifts 45-5 per cent.
All mines work a shingle shift on Saturdays. Caledonia could produce one thousand tons in that shift, but during May the Saturday morning shifts averaged from 337 tons to 5S1 tons.
On May 27 only 63 producers out of a possible 120 reported for work. The tons produced per man on that day amounted to three-quarters of a ton compared with over two tons on a normal day.
Week-end absenteeism is but a more acute condition of non-attendance at work affecting the whole week. If producers would work steadily five days weekly, output could be increased 22 per cent over actual six day performances during May.
As indication of the attitude toward Saturday work, I may state that No. 16 colliery has worked only on two Saturdays this year because men did not turn out for work. Sydney Mines collieries, Princess and Florence, have not worked on a Saturday since February 13, 1943, for the same reason.

In the bill referring to the disposal of war assets-and I hope hon. members will consider this when we come to discuss that bill in committee-tremendous power is vested in the Minister of Munitions and Supply to do almost anything. He can override the corporation and the associated committee which is set up-

If the section were to stop there of course it would be impossible for parliament to delegate such power to a minister, and I am sure no minister would ask for it. In the succeeding subsections (a) to (1) both inclusive there is an attempt to limit the subject matter in connection with which the minister may make regulations. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Well, its antiquity does not make it any better. This, Mr. Chairman, is just a repetition of what Lord Hewart many years ago eloquently described as "the new despotism," and this practice has gone unchallenged until now members of parliament are accustomed to having ministers bring down legislation of this kind, and to being told that because it had been done previously times without number, therefore it was all right. That doctrine does not appeal to me, and I do not think it should appeal to the membership of this house. It is a rule of law, of course, in delegating powers, especially in the municipal sphere, the municipalities being creatures of the provincial legislatures, that authority may be granted by the provincial legislatures to cities and incorporated towns to make by-laws and regulations respecting certain subject matters. If hon. gentlemen have had any experience in municipal law, and I presume there are members of the legal profession here who have had such experience, they will know that the courts always construe those delegated powers very strictly; that unless the thing was within the ambit of the delegated authority, it does not become legal. Many by-laws have been passed by municipal legislators under such delegated authority which have not stood the test of the courts. But I venture to suggest that there is no such restraining power on whoever may be minister under this bill. Who will come into court; what opportunity will there be in any given case to test the validity of the powers exercised by a minister under this delegated authority? There will be no one. In the first place, these regulations are usually applied to veterans-which, by the way, is not defined in the act, and before this bill passes I should like to know who is to be a veteran-and these men are in no position to

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
contest regulations made by the minister which might have detrimental effects upon their fortunes. Certainly the taxpayers of this country, who have to foot the bill, have no locus standi in the courts to contest the validity of any regulations the minister may make. The result would seem to be, and I think this is apparent, that within the ambit of section 7 of this bill the minister becomes a law unto himself, and he is passing legislation. In principle I condemn that practice. It ought never to be delegated by parliament, except in its most plain and administrative features.
Here the minister is granted authority. Authority is delegated to him to exercise not only administrative but also executive functions, and, I venture to say, judicial functions. Has the minister ever looked into that situation? Did his advisers, when they drew up this bill, have in mind the fact that once it passes parliament they are given full control over everything and can do about it as they please in the days to come, in respect of the great responsibilities of the situation which will be created after this bill becomes law? The well-being of numberless men is left to the tender care-I am willing to use that expression in its proper sense; I am not satirical when I use it-of the minister. That means it is left to his advisers.
I do not like this type of legislation at all. I do not think the country will like it when it is fully seized of its implications. And I do not think any administration ought to ask parliament for authority of this kind. It is on a par with government by order in council, which never sees the light of day until after its enactment into law under the War Measures Act.
The whole thing is bad in principle; it is wrong in practice, and it ought not to be followed out by parliament without at least a protest. That is what I am making to-day. I make that protest against the underlying principles and theories of this legislation. I hope I shall receive some support. I do not for one moment, of course, hope to change the minister's opinion. And yet I know that in his heart he will admit that the theories I am trying to advance are sound in law, in fact, and in principle.
Therefore I do protest as strongly as I know how against parliament's delegating to ministers, not merely the powers of administration-because I think they have to have those powers-but powers executive and judicial which should never be vested in an individual minister.
This is a repetition of what has gone on for more than twenty years, by all governments, and it is time to call a halt. I could illustrate by an analogous case I have in mind, going back many years ago to the time when the government of this country was operating Canadian government railways, among which was the old Intercolonial Railway. This was before the days of the board of railway commissioners, now known as the board of transport commissioners. A man who was opening up a new class of shipments- to be exact, the first movement of pulpwood from New Brunswick to the state of Maine- applied to the traffic manager of the Intercolonial railway to fix rates. The rate was high-even in those days it was so considered, despite the low level of wages, salaries and operating expenses. It was so high that having regard to the price of the commodity at its destination this would-be shipper could not see his way clear to move the goods. What did he do? He went to the minister of railways of that day, who happened to be a good personal as well as a good political friend. The minister of railways, under the authority vested in him under the old act, fixed a rate which was below the cost of operation to the railway. I give that only by way of illustration.
The minister is going very far in asking for the authority which would be vested in him under section 7. If the request were limited purely to administrative matters, I would not have so much objection to it. But I do object to giving the minister executive authority to legislate, and authority to exercise judicial functions.

I raised this point before, and I was not able to get an answer at the time. There are quite a number of eximperials in this country who find themselves in a destitute position and for whom no provision is made for payment of any allowance similar in nature to the war veterans' allowance. I should like to find out from the minister whether consideration has been given to the inclusion of these men and their dependents. Only to-day I received a letter from the widow of an imperial not in receipt of a pension at the time of his death. She is in destitute circumstances, and I know of no provision to-day whereby her condition may be alleviated. Is consideration being given to some award in the nature of the war veterans' allowances to such persons, or to their dependents?
There is another matter in connection with which I consider there should be an addition to the powers contained in section 7 to make regulations; I refer to a form of soldiers' insurance similar to that now in effect in the United States. So far as our pension department is concerned-and I am not inclined to hand out commendation unless I believe it is due-any matters I have brought to the minister's attention have received at all times
sympathetic consideration. If there is one thing more than another which we must endeavour to achieve in connection with veterans' matters, it is to remove them entirely from partisan consideration, and it is in that spirit that I discuss matters which I bring before the committee to-day.
In the United States there is in effect an insurance system under which any man who joins the army of the United States is entitled under the national service life insurance act of 1940 to apply for life insurance up to $10,000, for which the soldier pays at the rate of $7.70 per $1,000 per month for the period of hostilities. Should that soldier be killed in action or die while in the service of his country, payment is made for the period of two hundred and forty successive months at the rate of $5.51 per thousand dollars of insurance to the dependent or whoever is named. It would not be costly to bring in this system of insurance for the soldiers, and it would be conducive to the improvement of the conditions of the relatives of those who are killed in action. Many of those who die in the service of their country leave relatives -mother and father, we will say-who were not dependents but who in the later years of the soldier's life, had he survived, would have had the benefits which all sons confer upon their parents. I know of two families who in this war have each lost sons. To-day these people are almost in destitution, although they were not dependent upon their sons. Had there been in effect a system of national insurance such as there is in the United States, those parents would have been assured for a period of twenty years of a reasonable monthly payment,
I again bring this matter to the attention of the minister and the committee. It is not yet too late to bring into effect this system of national life insurance. I have endeavoured to ascertain in the past from various ministers what is being done, and each has taken the stand that the matter is being considered but that it does not come directly under his department. To-day, however, with the unifying of functions under a veterans' department, the matter will rest squarely on the minister. I would appreciate it if he would place before the committee the attitude of the government towards the establishment of a system of insurance similar to that in effect in the United States. I have here a pamphlet issued by the war department of the United States entitled "Personal Affairs of Military Personnel and Aid to Their Dependents" in which is set out in detail the rights of men and women in the armed forces of the United States and among'other things it gives full
Department of Veterans' Affairs

particulars of the insurance scheme. A similar kind of booklet might very well be considered by the minister and published here in Canada for the benefit of the troops.

Is it? Well, the general remarks I was about to make are applicable to the whole bill. I take exception to the use of the word "pension" as applied to members of the armed forces who have suffered disability on service. I do not think the word "pension" is the accurate one to use in that case. I know that there is great difficulty in finding another word; but generally speaking, a pension is something that is paid to an individual after long service. After *men in the permanent service have served thirty-five years or have devoted their entire life to the services of their country, they receive a pension, whereas a citizen soldier who enlists and receives a wound or disability also receives what is called a pension. I have heard some people criticize the use of the word "pension" there. It is not really a pension in the sense of a pension for long service; it is a compensatory grant for a definite disability caused on service. I wish , the minister would give some consideration to differentiating between a
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

definite pension for long service and the grant for disability caused by actual wounds or injuries in combat service.
My next point has come up before in this committee. It has to do with the differentiation between the rates of the United Kingdom pension and the Canadian pension. I have taken up with the minister several cases of imperials who were rated on a definite percentage of disability. I have had correspondence with him in respect of one case where the individual was rated a hundred per cent disability. He was badly gassed and suffered from tuberculosis. He was able to do only light work and was just getting by. He fought with the imperials in the last war. Although he had some claim to Canadian domicile before that war, it has not been allowed either by the United Kingdom authorities or by the Canadian authorities. Because he served in the United Kingdom forces his pension is on the United Kingdom basis. There is no complaint about his being a hundred per cent disability. AH the Canadian pension boards who have seen him have agreed that he is a hundred per cent disability; but because he happened to serve in the United Kingdom forces the actual cash pension that he receives per month is on the United Kingdom rate, which is very much lower than Canadian rates; consequently he finds great difficulty in getting by. Although he has not had to appeal to charity, he is almost in that position. There must be hundreds of cases of the kind. The first thing that the minister who is in charge of this department should do is to make some reciprocal agreement with the United Kingdom authorities so that when a veteran emigrates from the United Kingdom we may be prepared to take on the differential between the United Kingdom pension and the Canadian pension.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am glad to find that the minister has reached the point where he is actually going to answer in parliament when questions are asked. Everything is to be wide open and answers are to be given. It was because of a tendency that he has adopted in so many cases in the past of refusing parliament information that I scanned this bill carefully. The minister says that the intention is now to have all these transactions under this legislation follow the principle of the goldfish bowl. That is most commendable. Furthermore, he says that he is going to answer for the transactions that take place and give full information. That certainly is an advance, a statement far beyond anything that has characterized the minister's attitude heretofore. It is only four or five weeks ago that I asked a question in this house as to the price of coal per ton sold to the Dundurn camp and the answer given was that it was not considered in the public interest to give unit prices. Very often members have received the answer that it is not in the public interest to furnish information, and it is natural therefore that we should go through the bill and scrutinize it carefully to assure that parliament shall insist on a full accounting.
As to the necessity for this legislation, we on this side of the house accept as a fact that it is necessary, in other words, that a War Assets Corporation should be set up. But we do decry the method whereby this corporation is being set up, for in effect it constitutes a body appointed by and responsible to the minister. I point out first that under section 10, subsection 2, the War Assets Corporation:
. . . shall consist of a board of not less than six directors appointed by the minister with the approval of the governor in council.

Surplus Crown Assets
To show the powers of the corporation, section 11 says:
The board, -noth the approval of the minister, shall designate one of the directors to be the president and one of the directors to be the vice-president of the corporation.
And section 12 says:
Subject to general or specific instructions given by the minister the corporation may, when so directed by the minister, (a) sell, exchange, lease, lend or otherwise dispose of or deal with surplus crown assets either gratuitously or for a consideration and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as the board may consider desirable.
In other words, this board, purporting to be an independent board carrying out the activities prescribed by the legislation, is in fact an automaton under the control of the minister. It will have no extensive authority unless it has the approval of the minister.
Let me pass on to section 17:
The corporation shall establish and maintain an accounting system satisfactory to the minister.
Then subsection 4:
The accounts of the corporation shall be audited by the auditor general of Canada and the audited statements of such accounts shall be included in the corporation's annual report.
I pause here to mention that the auditor general's audit, however, would not carry detailed references to transactions; it would deal with amounts without dealing with individual transactions. Then section 18 says:
The corporation shall . . . submit an annual report to the minister in such form as he may prescribe and the minister shall lay the said report before parliament.
However good the intentions of our present minister may be in regard to giving full answers to parliament, under this bill, parliament having abdicated its rights, could properly be refused any detailed information with regard to the transactions. In fact, looking over this bill and taking it in conjunction with the Aeronautics Act, I see a trend which I believe is dangerous, and the abdication, by legislation passed bjr parliament, of parliament's right to full information. People want to know that this legislation will be administered fairly, definitely and openly or, so that all who run may read.
We believe that the principles under which this measure should be administered-and they represent the attitude taken by the government of the United States-are that sales should be made as early as possible witho<ut disrupting normal trade; that there should be no sales or rentals of crown property to speculators and certainly none to promoters; that sales should
be made in the goldfish bowl manner, with records always available to public inspection. Furthermore, in the disposal of these assets the public should be so protected that the assets shall not fall into the possession of monopolies, and all businesses should have equal access to the surplus.
I believe, too, that in order to protect the rights of the people of Canada in some four billion dollars worth of assets there should be a representative of the Department of Justice on the board. In fact, I think this is one board upon which either the Minister of Justice or the deputy minister of justice should be a member so as to prevent monopoly in the disposal of these assets.
As I look over this bill, full as it is of loopholes, I think it should be submitted again to a committee for changes to be recommended. As a nation we have accepted bureaucracy in war time. This measure has to do with the activities of a government corporation to operate in peace tme, and as at present constituted it does not provide for control by parliament. It purports to do so in the letter of the law, but according to any strict interpretation, if at any time within the next three or four or five years any member of the house rises in his place and asks how a particular plant was disposed of, what was done with a certain surplus, the answer that tire minister can give, if this measure is passed, may be that all the information he is required to place before parliament is the annual report of the corporation and no more, and in any event that as he is not a member of the corporation, the informaton asked for is not available. Before we grant power to the minister to take such a stand I feel that this committee and the country should realize the purport of the legislation as it now stands.
As I look over this bill and examine it together with the aeronautics bill I believe I can safely say that these two bills are deliberately or unintentionally colliding head-on with parliamentary and responsible government. We have accepted bureaucracy for the period of the war. This bill shows that bureaucracy is to be continued in time of peace. I believe that the time has come when parliament must limit and check government in manifestations such as these that indicate a trend toward the exercise by government corporations of unlimited power and a failure to recognize their responsibility to parliament. The minister says to-day: "I will furnish the information at any time." The bill does not indicate that some subsequent minister not so well-intentioned as the Minister of Munitions and
Surplus Crown Assets

Supply would do the same thing. Put in its simplest form this bill permits of the establishment by parliament of a corporation designated by the minister responsible not to parliament but to the minister, with the minister in the position of being able to say, *when questioned in parliament, that what was done was done by a corporation and that he had no knowledge of what that corporation had done.
I suggest that this bill as it now stands requires that certain further provisions be added to it to curtail the powers of this corporation, to require it to account to parliament, and to permit and to demand in fact, that this corporation shall make a report to parliament fully setting out in detail each and every transaction. If the minister is prepared to accept a suggestion I would say that any objection lo this bill can be removed by making provision in section 18 whereby in the annual report that is laid before parliament full details shall be given of all transactions that have taken place during the year being reported. If the minister will accept that suggestion then I feel the other objections I have raised will not be as tenable as they otherwise are.
What the members of this committee want is to control the activities of corporations that are nominated by the minister to the end that I he people of Canada shall be assured that in I he administration of the disposal of billions of dollars' worth of assets, the property of this dominion, proper principles shall be followed and that preference shall not be given by the corporation in favour of anyone; that the largest possible returns shall be insisted upon and that the War Assets Corporation shall not be vested with absolute power by reason of parliament abdicating the right to demand a full and proper accounting.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I stated a few moments ago that it would be the policy of the government to make full disclosure with regard to any and all transactions of the corporation being created by the bill that is now being considered by this committee. My hon. friend stated that he doubted whether a full disclosure was to be made because the department had refused to give the unit prices for the purchase of coal at Dundurn camp. May I point out to my hon. friend that the difference in the two transactions is that the government is a buyer of coal. It buys coal by open tender. The objection to giving the prices is that the prices could be of no value to a member of parliament, but they could be of great value to another coal dealer. The Department of Munitions and Supply is a buyer of a vast

number of things, and has adopted the policy of not disclosing tenders. That I think has saved the government money. Any coal dealer who desires to obtain the Dundurn contract must sharpen his pencil and put in the lowest price that he can possibly put together. If he does that he has a chance of getting the business. If the unit prices of the lowest tender were disclosed, they would be a guide to any dealer, and the chances are that that dealer would not sharpen his pencil as much as he would if he did not know the objective he was trying to reach. That is the difference between the government as a buyer and the government as a seller. As a seller the government should gladly make known its prices, because there the position is that the government desirps to get the highest possible price for its equipment and there is everything to be gained from disclosure, whereas nothing is to be gained by disclosure where the government is a buyer.
The hon. gentleman objected to the responsibilities imposed upon the minister. At that stage I thought he was making a speech in favour of bureaucracy, for he seemed to object to the minister setting the policy of the corporation, and to the provision that all transactions should be made either by direction of the minister or with his approval. The latter, of course, is parliamentary responsibility. A corporation cannot be responsible to parliament; there is no machinery for that, except through a minister of the crown. Under this bill the minister must keep himself advised of all major transactions and must direct the selling policy of the corporation. The minister sits in parliament and is subject to questioning by parliament. Under the terms of this bill he can never fall back on the answer that the corporation is not directly answerable to parliament through him. The fact of the matter is, however, that the report is never opened for discussion, unless at some future time an opportunity may be afforded when some other item is under discussion.
We have a number of government corporations or institutions. Sometimes they are called arms of government. Sometimes they are described as government corporations, and sometimes as institutions. These various institutions make reports to parliament, and have in their acts sections such as the one now before us. The Canadian National Railways is a government organization, and reports to parliament. Its report is placed upon the table of the house. In respect of that institution a special committee of parliament scrutinizes very carefully its operations.
Then we have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, another government institution. While there is no standing committee on radio broadcasting, radio has grown to a place in Canadian life where it has been found advisable to have a special committee to deal with the annual report of that corporation.
We have another institution known as the Bank of Canada, which lays its reports upon the table, through the appropriate minister. But when is that report discussed by parliament? The standing committee would make its report to parliament on the basis of its findings. Concurrence would be moved, and a discussion could take place. To my mind that is the only sensible procedure. I do not know that a provision of that kind could be put in this legislation, or that we could add anything to this section which would set up a committee. I suggest, however, that the government should bring down the appropriate legislation having for its purpose the setting up of a standing committee for the purpose of scrutinizing the activities of corporations' of this kind. That would be my suggestion for the solution of this matter.

No parliament is bound by the decisions of a previous parliament, because legislation passed by one parliament may be, and frequently is, amended by another. The point raised by the parliamentary assistant seems to me an ingenious method of attempting to rule out an amendment which has as its aim to give parliament some supervision and some powers of inquiry and investigation with resepct to the matters under review.
The difficulty which most hon. members, I think, find in section 18 as it stands is that the report is almost entirely in the hands of the minister, and that of course is what the hon. member for Lake Centre is attempting to obviate. Sell War Assets to Consumers as Far as Possible.

They are greatly concerned about this, and I think now would be the time for the minister to give the municipalities some further assurance that the local governments will be given first claim on any machinery or property under the control of this corporation which is now being set up. subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:

For instance, the first claim on material of use to a province would be the provincial claim, and the second would be the municipal claim. Priorities would be given as recommended by the committee, which is a feature of this bill. It is not the purpose of the corporation to give away anything. Its purpose is to dispose of government property in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole, and the only possible procedure is to place a price on the property or equipment and to give priorities where priorities are due, but to sell at one price to all. Governments of provinces and municipal governments have always paid for their equipment; they are well able to pay for it, and I think all that they can

(a) , sell, exchange, lease, lend-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The question I have in mind is this. As I read the bill, powers are conferred on the Minister of Munitions and Supply giving him the right to do as he pleases, regardless of what the corporation wishes or decides to do. I read first section 10, subsection 6:
The corporation shall be responsible to. and he subject to the direction and control of, the minister.
Then section 22 says that the minister, without regard to the corporation, may execute on behalf of His Majesty any deed, contract or document transferring title to any surplus
{Mr. Howe.]
crown assets other than a grant of land, and whenever such document has been so executed it is valid and binding upon His Majesty.
As I read those two sections they confer on the minister the right to dispose of any of the property of the War Assets Corporation without regard to the members of that corporation. If, for instance, the corporation wishes or decides to dispose of certain property to party "A" and the minister does not agree and says that the property should go to party "B", he may not only overrule the corporation set up by this parliament but proceed without regard to the officers of the corporation to execute the necessary documents giving title to the party chosen by himself. I think, with all due respect to the minister, that is conferring a power upon him never before conferred upon any minister in this or any other country. It gives him the absolute right to decide, regardless of the corporation, on the disposal of billions of dollars worth of assets. If that is the meaning, and I can see no other meaning, 1 think some limitation should be placed upon such absqlute power.
When you read the bill generally you see that the corporation is given certain powers, but then w'hen you read section 22 you find that the minister has the absolute and final say, regardless of the wishes of the corporation set up by this parliament. He may himself determine, without control and untrammeled the disposal of these assets. I do not know1 why such powers must of necessity be conferred upon the minister. It is a tremendous power to place in the hands of any one man. Not only is it tremendous in its implications, but when one considers the assets to be disposed of one realizes that it makes the Minister of Munitions and Supply more powerful than any other minister in any representative government, has ever been. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that better reasons than have been given should be given why this power, unlimited in extent and uncontrolled by the corporation, should be conferred upon the minister. If we confer such absolute power on the minister of any representative government we cannot complain in this parliament afterwards if the powers are exercised in a way that we did not expect. I submit that such unlimited power ought not to be conferred upon a minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is fair, because first he denounces bureaucracy and then he denounces ministerial control. He made quite a speech against bureaucracy, against giving the corporation complete authority. Now he

Surplus Crown Assets
denounces ministerial control, which is undoubtedly preserved by these provisions, and I think, rightly so. The powers of the minister are only exercisable with the approval of the government of which he is a member. speechtext:
(York-Sunbury): I wonder if this is the position. On reading the bill one would assume at first blush that the government was setting up a corporation and then allocating to it the duty of disposing of surplus assets. When one gets down to cases and specific instances one finds that this corporation is merely a selling agency, that there is an overpowering veto in the hands of the minister who, notwithstanding any recommendation of the corporation, may say, "No, you must not do that; you must do thus and so."
I do not understand why the minister desires to delegate authority, on the one hand, and pull it back, on the other. It may be that he visualizes situations arising where it may be necessary to do that, but if he has a company officered by outstanding business men in whom he has confidence, why should he not allow those men to proceed, once an order in council has been passed, in the case of surplus assets exceeding $15,000, and without an order in council, where they are under that limit? If those men are of the proper type, why not give them free scope to go ahead? I am not going to raise a row about the matter, but on the theories that I have advanced it is simply giving with the one hand and withholding with the other.
I would suppose that it would be better to have the disposition of these goods in the hands of men who are not influenced by any ulterior consideration such as might be imposed upon the minister by his followers or what-not. We know how those things happen. I just wish the minister would1 go a little farther than he has and state whether or not I have correctly visualized the position, that on the one hand he is designating an agent and on the other he is keeping control over what they will do. They may just as well be
considered as factors. That is all they would be as long as the minister keeps his hand on the situation.
I should like to call the attention of the minister to section 23 which contains some of the most extraordinary provisions I have ever seen in a statute of this kind. It states:
The governor in council may:
(a)	make such orders as he may deem necessary or desirable with reference to the organization, administration or management of the committee or corporation and to confer on the committee or corporation additional powers and duties.
I gather that those are in addition to the powers conferred by the bill itself. What is contemplated by paragraph (a) of section 23? What additional powers and duties are to be conferred on the committee or corporation? The next paragraph reads:
(b)	make or issue such orders, rules and regulations as may be deemed necessary or desirable to assist the minister to exercise and perform the duties conferred or imposed upon him by or pursuant to this act.
If you read it apart from the limiting clause the corporation can do anything. It looks to me as being redundant. The draftsman of this bill must have had something in mind and I am going to ask the minister to tell us frankly why those two clauses are interpolated at the tail end of this bill.
Has the minister given any consideration to the suggestion I made on the second reading that the net proceeds from the disposition of these surplus assets shall be devoted only to the reduction of the national debt? For the most part these goods have been bought and paid for with borrowings which have been added to the public debt, and the proceeds should not go into consolidated revenue fund. I think that is a basic financial principle which the minister will at once recognize and accede to, but there is nothing in this bill to cover that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In reply to the first point raised by my hon. friend may I say that in my opinion there is nothing worse than authority without responsibility, or the reverse, responsibility without authority. Since the minister must necessarily retain the responsibility for all the acts of the corporation, he should not divorce himself of all authority, particularly the authority of veto. The purpose of the corporation is to gather together men possessing information and experience which no minister could have, to guide the minister in the proper administration and sale of these assets. I think that purpose will be served with the bill as it is drawn to-day.
Surplus Crown Assets

My hon. friend is inquiring as to what additional authority will be required. Section 12 of the bill gives the corporation powers which are considered to be adequate, but this bill is providing for work of a type which has never been previously undertaken by a crown corporation, and it has been thought well to give the governor in council authority to confer additional powers on the corporation if experience proves that they are required.
The third matter raised is as to how the funds recovered from the sale of the assets will be used. Under this bill the minister is to pay these funds into the consolidated revenue fund. It will be a matter for the Minister of Finance of the day, or the government of the day, to determine how the funds so realized will be used. I do not think my hon. friend can expect the minister designated to administer this measure to decide how the funds shall be used.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I would not suggest that, but I suggest that parliament should now give him a lead. We should put in the bill the provision that that is to be done. I think it would be bad for public financing if the net proceeds from the sales of these surplus assets, either through the agency of the corporation or through the activities of the minister, were to be allowed to go into consolidated revenue fund and then be paid out for any purpose which parliament might subsequently vote. These moneys have been borrowed and interest is being paid thereon. The public debt has been increased. These are capital assets in the true sense of the word, having regard to their origin. The proceeds of the sale of these capital assets should be earmarked for debt reduction and I challenge anybody to contradict the soundness of that theory.

There might be some argument why the minister should reserve himself the right to do so, but I cannot see any argument in favour, not only of reserving the right to himself, but also of setting up some other corporation or of giving somebody else specifically or generally the power of disposal.
